name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
title: Model Risk and Bias Testing
answer: Model risk and bias testing covers the checks an organisation runs on a model before and after it goes into use, to see whether it produces wrong, unstable or unfairly skewed outputs. It spans statistical validation, outcome testing across groups, documentation of assumptions and limits, and ongoing monitoring once the model is live. In an accounting or financial data setting it applies to credit scoring, fraud detection, forecasting and any model whose output feeds a decision about a person or a ledger.

sections.body: Model risk and bias testing covers the checks an organisation runs on a model before and after it goes into use, to see whether it produces wrong, unstable or unfairly skewed outputs. It spans statistical validation, outcome testing across groups, documentation of assumptions and limits, and ongoing monitoring once the model is live. In an accounting or financial data setting it applies to credit scoring, fraud detection, forecasting and any model whose output feeds a decision about a person or a ledger.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of data platforms, model registries and testing pipelines. Teams typically need a governed copy of the training and production data, a versioned store of model artefacts, and compute to rerun a model against held out or sliced datasets. Logging and lineage tools matter as much as the modelling stack, because a test result is only useful if it can be tied back to the exact data and model version that produced it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by defining what the model is for and which groups or scenarios could be harmed if it fails. They then run quantitative checks such as error rates by subgroup, calibration, stability over time and sensitivity to small input changes, alongside qualitative review of the data and the assumptions behind it. Findings are documented with the evidence, the thresholds used and the residual uncertainty, and results are re-run when the model, the data or the population it serves changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership, approval and evidence retention sit with risk, compliance and internal audit rather than the modelling team alone. Regulators and auditors expect a documented testing standard, an independent challenge to the developer's own results, and a clear record of who accepted which limitation and when. Where personal or financial data is used, testing has to respect privacy rules, access controls and retention limits, and the same discipline applies to third party or vendor models that the organisation did not build.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Testing is moving from a one-off exercise at sign-off toward continuous monitoring wired into production, with automated alerts when a model drifts or a subgroup's error rate moves. Expect more emphasis on documenting the testing of generative and third party models, on evidence that survives audit, and on tooling that keeps a defensible trail from data through to decision. The direction is toward fewer manual reports and more repeatable, versioned checks that a reviewer can inspect on demand.
